title: What a Market Is
objective: After this level you can explain a market as any place where buyers and sellers meet.
summary: A market is any way buyers and sellers get in contact to trade, from a village grocer to a website. eBay's first sale, a broken laser pointer, shows how a big market finds a buyer for almost anything.

cards.headline: In 1995, a broken laser pointer sold online for $14.83.
cards.body: It didn't work, and somebody paid for it anyway. That sale was the first on the website that became eBay. To see why it makes sense, you need to know what a market really is.

cards.headline: A meeting, not a place
cards.body: Picture a market and you probably see stalls and shouting. Economists mean something wider: any way buyers and sellers get in contact to swap goods and services, face to face or through go-betweens. A village grocer counts. So does a website. In a modern economy, the market isn't a place at all. It's wherever sellers compete for your money.

cards.headline: The laser pointer finds its buyer
cards.body: Pierre Omidyar launched AuctionWeb over Labor Day weekend in 1995, and his broken laser pointer sold for $14.83. Remember Level 2's mechanic hunting for a farmer with a broken car? Omidyar had no such problem. The buyer paid in money, so Omidyar didn't need anything the buyer owned. He needed just one person, anywhere, who wanted a broken laser pointer. A big enough market finds that person.

cards.fact: Markets trade far more than things. There are markets for work and for savings.
cards.context: Supply and demand, this chapter's big idea, work in any market. In a labor market, job seekers supply work and employers demand it. In a financial market, savers supply money and borrowers demand it. And as trade in goods grew, financial markets like stock exchanges multiplied too.

cards.headline: Markets: mapped
learned: A market is any way buyers and sellers meet
It doesn't need a place: a website counts
Money means you only need one willing buyer
There are markets for goods, work and savings

questions.prompt: To an economist, what is a market?

options.label: A building full of stalls selling food
options.rationale: That is one kind of market, but a market needs no building.

options.label: Any way buyers and sellers get in contact to trade
A list of prices set by the government
options.rationale: A market is where buyers and sellers meet, not a price list.

options.label: Only the big stock exchanges
options.rationale: Those are markets, but so is the village grocer.

questions.explanation: A market is any means by which buyers and sellers get in contact, directly or through go-betweens. It need not be a place.

questions.prompt: In a labor market, who is doing the supplying?

options.label: Employers, who supply jobs
options.rationale: Employers are the buyers: they demand work.

options.label: Job seekers, who supply their work
Shoppers, who supply money
options.rationale: Shoppers are buyers in markets for goods.

questions.explanation: In a labor market, job seekers supply work and employers demand it.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: why didn't Omidyar need a double coincidence of wants to sell his laser pointer?

options.label: The buyer paid money, so Omidyar needed nothing the buyer had
The buyer also had a broken laser pointer to swap
options.rationale: No swap happened: the buyer paid in money.

options.label: eBay set the price for both of them
options.rationale: The price came from the auction, not from eBay.

options.label: Laser pointers were legal tender in 1995
options.rationale: They were never money; dollars were.

questions.explanation: With money in the middle, a seller only needs someone who wants the item, not someone who also has what the seller wants.
